title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 6: Digitally Integrated Care Pathways for Multiple-Long-Term-Conditions in Sri Lanka

description.narrative:
A UK and low- and middle-income country (LMIC) research partnership that aims to improve the management of multiple long-term conditions in primary care in Sri Lanka.
Long-term health conditions are becoming increasingly more common in low-and-middle-income countries, leading to disability and early death. In Sri Lanka, many people suffer from diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, kidney disease, and mental health conditions. When someone has several long-term conditions, it becomes more difficult to manage their care, leading to poor health outcomes.
The project plans to use electronic patient record systems in primary care centres to create an improved care plan for those with multiple long-term conditions. This plan is called a digitally integrated care pathway (DICP). It aims to standardise care and improve the patient experience using digital technologies. The research project has six parts, or "work-packages (WP)," which will lead to the development and evaluation of the DICP for patients with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, chronic kidney disease, depression, and anxiety.
In the first part (WP1), a group of people, including patients, doctors, and policymakers, will be brought together to help create the DICP. They will make sure it meets the needs of patients and healthcare providers and that it can be used across the country. In another part (WP2), we will understand the current healthcare pathways in Sri Lanka and get input from local patients and healthcare professionals to make improvements. They will choose the best guidelines for care, so doctors and nurses know how best to support the care of people with multiple long-term conditions.
The DICP will have four key parts developed (WP3), that will connect to an electronic patient record system called OpenMRS. It will include digital guidelines, so doctors have the best information for treatment. There will be a digital referral system for communication and collaboration among healthcare providers. Automated feedback to clinicians will help improve the quality of care. Finally, there will be a digital patient-facing interface for patients to access their health information and take an active role in their care.
To see how well the DICP works, we will test it in 50 primary care centres using a special study called a cluster randomised controlled trial (WP4). We will also see if it is worth using in other parts of the country. The project will train and support a group of local experts to lead the use of the DICP and improve the care of people with multiple long-term health conditions in Sri Lanka. The research ultimately aims to improve healthcare for these patients and the use of digital technologies to make it easier to provide the right care at the right time.

Our aim is to develop, implement and evaluate a digitally integrated care pathway (DICP) within electronic health records (EHRs) to manage primary care patients with multiple long-term conditions (MLTC) in Sri Lanka. Our focus will be on diabetes, hypertension and associated cardiometabolic, renal and mental health conditions.
We will achieve our aims through the following objectives:
1. To establish a stakeholder consultation group (SCG) consisting of people living with MLTC, healthcare professionals, clinical informaticians, policy makers and researchers to provide expertise throughout the research lifecycle
2. To evaluate existing care pathways and clinical guidelines and identify stakeholder priorities for improvement
3. To develop and implement a stakeholder designed DICP
4. To evaluate the DICP through a cluster randomised controlled trial
5. To evaluate the contextual and organisational factors that may influence scalability and transferability of the DICP across Sri Lanka and countries with similar population and health systems
6. To carry out an economic evaluation of the DICP
